    Chapter 10

    Key Exchange: Agreeing on a Secret in Public

    🤔 Two strangers shout numbers across a crowded room, and end up sharing a secret that nobody else in the room can work out.

    • ⏱️ ~6 min
    • 📚 9 sections
    • 🎮 4 interactive
    • ⭐ 235 XP
    • 🔑 1 fragment

    10.1The puzzle#

    Alice and Bob have never met. Every word they send can be heard by Eve. Can they agree on a secret key that Eve doesn't learn?

    It sounds impossible. In 1976, Whitfield Diffie and Martin Hellman showed how to do it. Their method, Diffie-Hellman key exchange, runs every time you open a secure website, make a WhatsApp call or connect to a VPN.

    ✔ section read

    10.2The paint-mixing analogy#

    Imagine that mixing paint is easy, but separating mixed paint back into its colors is impossible.

    Eve saw yellow, orange and green. To make brown she needs red or blue, which never left Alice's or Bob's house. She can't "unmix" orange to get red.

    ✏️ sketching an interactive demo…
    ✔ section read

    10.3The real math, with tiny numbers#

    In real Diffie-Hellman, "mixing paint" is modular exponentiation (Chapter 3): easy forward, practically impossible backward.

    Step Alice Public (Eve sees) Bob
    1. Agree on public numbers prime p = 23, base g = 5
    2. Pick a secret a = 6 (secret) b = 15 (secret)
    3. Compute public value A = 5⁶ mod 23 = 8 B = 5¹⁵ mod 23 = 19
    4. Exchange sends A = 8 ──► A = 8, B = 19 ◄── sends B = 19
    5. Compute shared secret B^a = 19⁶ mod 23 = 2 A^b = 8¹⁵ mod 23 = 2

    Both get 2. Eve knows p = 23, g = 5, A = 8 and B = 19, but to find the secret she'd need a or b, which means solving the discrete logarithm problem. With 23 that's easy. With a 2048-bit prime (617 digits), it's out of reach.

    🧮 Why both get the same answer: Alice computes (g^b)^a and Bob computes (g^a)^b. Both equal g^(a×b), because multiplying exponents doesn't care about order. That's the entire trick.

    Python
    p, g = 23, 5
a, b = 6, 15                 # secrets
A = pow(g, a, p)             # 8   (Alice sends)
B = pow(g, b, p)             # 19  (Bob sends)
print(pow(B, a, p))          # 2   (Alice's result)
print(pow(A, b, p))          # 2   (Bob's result)

    10.4Diffie-Hellman in the real world#

    Variant Math Key size Notes
    Finite-field DH (DHE) Modular exponentiation with huge primes 2048–4096 bits Older; still supported. Standard prime groups like ffdhe2048 are defined in RFC 7919.
    ECDH (ECDHE) Elliptic curves, e.g. P-256 256 bits Widely used in TLS
    X25519 Curve25519 32-byte keys ✅ The most common choice today: fast, simple, safe
    X25519MLKEM768 X25519 + post-quantum ML-KEM ~1.2 KB of key data ✅ The new default in browsers (section 10.8)

    The "E" at the end of DHE or ECDHE means ephemeral, explained in section 10.6.

    ⚖️ Pros & Cons

    Key-exchange variants

    ⚠️ Legacy
    Finite-field DHE

    Big primes, 2048–4096 bits

    • Simple math, old and well understood
    • Forward secrecy when ephemeral
    • Large and slow
    • Weak or shared groups caused Logjam
    Best for: Legacy compatibility
    ✅ Use it
    ECDHE (P-256)

    Elliptic-curve DH

    • Small and fast
    • FIPS-friendly
    • Must validate received points
    Best for: Regulated environments
    ✅ Use it
    X25519

    Curve25519 DH

    • 32-byte keys, very fast
    • Any 32 bytes is a valid key: fewer pitfalls
    • Not quantum-safe on its own
    Best for: The default classical choice
    ✅ Use it
    X25519MLKEM768

    Hybrid classical + post-quantum

    • Attacker must break both
    • Stops harvest-now-decrypt-later
    • Default in major browsers
    • ~1.2 KB of key data per handshake
    • Newer code paths
    Best for: Any connection carrying long-lived secrets
    ❌ Avoid
    Static RSA key transport

    TLS_RSA_WITH_…

    • Simple; old
    • No forward secrecy
    • Bleichenbacher/ROBOT
    • Removed from TLS 1.3
    Best for: Nowhere

    10.5The catch: man-in-the-middle attacks#

    Diffie-Hellman protects against Eve (who only listens). It does not, on its own, protect against Mallory (who can intercept and modify messages).

    Mallory sits in the middle and runs two separate key exchanges: one with Alice (pretending to be Bob) and one with Bob (pretending to be Alice).

    Alice thinks she's talking securely to Bob. She is talking securely, to Mallory.

    The fix: authentication. Alice needs to know that the value B really came from Bob. Ways to do that:

    1. Digital signatures + certificates (how HTTPS does it): the server signs its key-exchange value with its long-term private key, and a certificate from a trusted authority proves that the public key belongs to that website. (Chapters 11, 13 and 14.)
    2. Verify fingerprints in person or by another channel: Signal's "safety numbers" and SSH's "host key fingerprint" prompts (Chapters 15 and 16).
    3. A pre-shared secret or password, as in WPA3 Wi-Fi (Chapter 15).

    💡 Key idea: Key exchange gives you a shared secret. Authentication tells you who you share it with. You need both. Unauthenticated encryption is like whispering secrets to a stranger in a dark room.

    10.6Ephemeral keys and forward secrecy#

    Older HTTPS often used RSA key transport: the browser generated a secret, encrypted it with the server's long-term RSA public key, and sent it.

    That has a nasty weakness. Suppose an attacker records your encrypted traffic today. Years later, they steal (or legally demand) the server's private key. Now they can decrypt the recorded secret and every recorded conversation, going back years.

    Ephemeral Diffie-Hellman fixes this. For every single connection:

    1. Both sides generate a brand-new Diffie-Hellman key pair.
    2. They derive the session key from it.
    3. When the connection ends, they delete the temporary private keys.

    The server's long-term key is used only to sign the exchange (to prove identity), not to protect the secret itself. If that long-term key is stolen later, the attacker can impersonate the server in the future, but they can't decrypt past sessions, because the ephemeral keys no longer exist anywhere.

    This property is called forward secrecy (or "perfect forward secrecy," PFS).

    Analogy: instead of using the same padlock for every conversation, you use a disposable padlock for each one and melt it down afterwards.

    📜 Why it matters: documents leaked in 2013 described intelligence agencies recording vast amounts of encrypted internet traffic to decrypt later. The industry responded by switching to forward secrecy. TLS 1.3 (2018) requires it: RSA key transport was removed entirely.

    ⚖️ Pros & Cons

    Ephemeral vs. static keys

    ✅ Use it
    Ephemeral (DHE/ECDHE)

    Fresh keys per session, then deleted

    • Forward secrecy
    • A stolen server key can’t decrypt past recordings
    • A key exchange for every connection
    • Can’t passively decrypt for monitoring (a feature!)
    Best for: Every modern protocol
    ❌ Avoid
    Static

    Same key for years

    • Simpler
    • Enables passive decryption for debugging
    • One stolen key decrypts everything, past and future
    Best for: Avoid for traffic encryption
    ✔ section read

    10.7KEMs: a different style of key agreement#

    A Key Encapsulation Mechanism (KEM) reaches the same goal in a slightly different way. Instead of both sides contributing a value, one side generates a random secret and "wraps" it for the other side's public key:

    This is the shape of the new post-quantum algorithm ML-KEM (formerly called Kyber), standardized by NIST in 2024 as FIPS 203.

    ⚖️ Pros & Cons

    Diffie-Hellman vs. KEM

    ✅ Use it
    Diffie-Hellman

    Both sides contribute

    • Symmetric, elegant
    • Tiny with X25519
    • No lattice-based DH is practical yet
    Best for: Classical key agreement
    ✅ Use it
    KEM

    One side wraps a fresh secret

    • Fits post-quantum math (ML-KEM)
    • Clean API: encapsulate / decapsulate
    • Bigger messages (ML-KEM-768 ciphertext is 1,088 bytes)
    Best for: Post-quantum and HPKE
    ✔ section read

    10.8Post-quantum key exchange is already here#

    A large enough quantum computer could break X25519, ECDH and RSA (Chapter 17). Nobody has one yet, but recorded traffic could be decrypted later ("harvest now, decrypt later"). So the industry is already using hybrid key exchange:

    An attacker would have to break both to recover the key. This hybrid, named X25519MLKEM768, is enabled by default in current Chrome, Edge and Firefox, in Cloudflare's network, and in OpenSSL 3.5 and later.

    You can see it yourself: when this guide's examples were tested, OpenSSL 3.6 connecting to www.google.com reported Negotiated TLS1.3 group: X25519MLKEM768.

    ✔ section read

    10.9Hands-on with key exchange#

    🧪 Try it yourself (OpenSSL): Alice and Bob each make a key pair, swap public keys, and compute the same secret.

    Terminal
    # Each person generates an X25519 key pair
openssl genpkey -algorithm X25519 -out alice_x.pem
openssl genpkey -algorithm X25519 -out bob_x.pem

# Each extracts their public key and "sends" it to the other
openssl pkey -in alice_x.pem -pubout -out alice_x_pub.pem
openssl pkey -in bob_x.pem   -pubout -out bob_x_pub.pem

# Alice combines HER private key with BOB's public key
openssl pkeyutl -derive -inkey alice_x.pem -peerkey bob_x_pub.pem -out alice_secret.bin

# Bob combines HIS private key with ALICE's public key
openssl pkeyutl -derive -inkey bob_x.pem -peerkey alice_x_pub.pem -out bob_secret.bin

# Compare: identical 32-byte secrets
xxd -p -c 64 alice_secret.bin
xxd -p -c 64 bob_secret.bin
cmp alice_secret.bin bob_secret.bin && echo "SAME SECRET"

    In Python, including the HKDF step that turns the raw shared secret into a proper encryption key:

    Python
    from cryptography.hazmat.primitives.asymmetric.x25519 import X25519PrivateKey
from cryptography.hazmat.primitives.kdf.hkdf import HKDF
from cryptography.hazmat.primitives import hashes

alice_private = X25519PrivateKey.generate()
bob_private   = X25519PrivateKey.generate()

# Public keys are exchanged over the open internet
alice_public = alice_private.public_key()
bob_public   = bob_private.public_key()

alice_shared = alice_private.exchange(bob_public)
bob_shared   = bob_private.exchange(alice_public)
print(alice_shared == bob_shared)            # True

# Never use the raw secret directly as a key: run it through a KDF
session_key = HKDF(algorithm=hashes.SHA256(), length=32,
                   salt=None, info=b"my-chat-app v1").derive(alice_shared)

    If you have OpenSSL 3.5 or later, you can also generate post-quantum keys and see how much bigger they are:

    Terminal
    openssl genpkey -algorithm ML-KEM-768 -out mlkem.pem
openssl pkey -in mlkem.pem -pubout -outform DER | wc -c    # ~1206 bytes (vs 44 for X25519)
